domainCoverage.synopsis: Modern security assumes internal networks are already compromised. This volume establishes zero-trust architecture, cryptographic identity (mTLS), OAuth2/OIDC token governance, and OWASP defense-in-depth.

chapters.title: Encryption at Rest & in Transit
chapters.summary: Encryption in transit protects data moving across untrusted networks via TLS 1.3/mTLS, while encryption at rest protects persisted disks and backups using AES-256-GCM envelope encryption backed by a KMS.

chapters.title: Zero Trust Networking
chapters.summary: Zero-trust networking replaces implicit IP- and VLAN-based perimeter trust with cryptographic workload identity (SPIFFE/mTLS), continuous device/user attestation, and per-request L7 authorization (Envoy/OPA) on every hop.

chapters.title: OAuth2, JWT & Mutual TLS (mTLS) Security Architecture
chapters.summary: Modern API security pairs OAuth 2.0 (for delegated user/client authorization), signed JWTs (for stateless, verifiable claims), and Mutual TLS (mTLS) (for cryptographic workload and high-assurance client identity).

chapters.title: OAuth2 Authorization Flows
chapters.summary: OAuth 2.0 delegates scoped API access without sharing user passwords, using distinct grant flows tailored to confidential backends, public SPAs/mobile apps, headless devices, and service-to-service workloads. Modern OAuth 2.1 deprecates the Implicit and Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC) flows in favor of Authorization Code + PKCE.

chapters.title: OpenID Connect Identity
chapters.summary: An interoperable identity layer built on top of OAuth 2.0 that issues cryptographically signed JWT ID Tokens so applications can verify who a user is.

chapters.title: JWT Validation Pitfalls
chapters.summary: Stateless JSON Web Tokens fail catastrophically when verifiers trust header fields (`alg`, `kid`, `jku`), skip audience/issuer checks, or confuse asymmetric public keys with HMAC secrets.

chapters.title: MFA & Risk-Based Authentication
chapters.summary: Risk-based Multi-Factor Authentication (RBA) evaluates contextual telemetry—device posture, ASN/GeoIP, impossible travel, and TLS fingerprints—in real time to dynamically step up high-risk logins to phishing-resistant WebAuthn/FIDO2 while keeping trusted sessions frictionless.

chapters.title: RBAC Policy Design
chapters.summary: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) decouples permissions from individual users by grouping privileges into named roles, simplifying least-privilege governance and auditing at scale.

chapters.title: Secrets Management & Vaults
chapters.summary: A centralized secrets manager like HashiCorp Vault encrypts static credentials behind a Shamir-unsealed barrier and issues short-lived, dynamically generated credentials (e.g., 1-hour PostgreSQL roles or 15-minute STS tokens) via workload identity (Kubernetes JWT/IAM) with automatic lease revocation.

chapters.title: SQL Injection Prevention
chapters.summary: SQL injection (CWE-89) happens when untrusted input is concatenated into a SQL string, letting attackers alter query structure; preventing it requires strict code-data separation via parameterized queries (prepared statements), allowlists for dynamic identifiers, and least-privilege database roles.

chapters.title: XSS & Content Security Policy
chapters.summary: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) lets attackers execute arbitrary JavaScript in a victim's browser origin; Content Security Policy (CSP Level 3) acts as defense-in-depth by restricting script execution to cryptographically random per-request nonces and Trusted Types.

chapters.title: CSRF Defense Patterns
chapters.summary: CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) tricks an authenticated user's browser into sending unintended state-changing requests to a target origin that automatically attaches ambient session cookies.

domainDeepDive.whatIsThisDomain: Application and infrastructure security establishes the defensive perimeter, cryptographic identity, and access control invariants of modern distributed platforms. It encompasses zero-trust network microsegmentation, mutual TLS (mTLS) cryptographic handshakes, OAuth2/OIDC token governance, fine-grained Role-Based and Attribute-Based Access Control (RBAC/ABAC), and defense-in-depth against injection, forgery, and supply chain attacks.
domainDeepDive.whyItMatters: Security breaches inflict catastrophic and often fatal damage on organizations: compromised customer data, regulatory penalties (GDPR/HIPAA/PCI-DSS), ransom demands, and irreparable brand erosion. In modern architectures, assuming that internal corporate networks are secure is a fatal fallacy. Engineers must design systems under the assumption that the network is hostile, external perimeter firewalls have been breached, and every service call must cryptographically verify identity and authority.
domainDeepDive.keyTakeaway: Assume the internal network is already compromised. Eliminate ambient trust, enforce cryptographic identity (mTLS) and least privilege for every hop, validate input contexts strictly, and fail closed by default.
coreArchitectureRules: Zero-Trust Architecture Invariant: Never trust, always verify. Every network connection, whether coming from the public internet or an adjacent internal microservice, must be mutually authenticated and explicitly authorized.

Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP): Every user, service, and background process must be granted the minimal set of permissions necessary to execute its specific function, and for the shortest duration necessary.

Complete Input Parameterization & Contextual Sanitization: Never construct SQL queries, HTML strings, or shell commands via string concatenation. Treat all external input as malicious and parameterize at the driver boundary.

Cryptographic Freshness & Nonce Verification: Every security token, signature, and sensitive protocol interaction must incorporate timestamps, expiration limits, and unique cryptographic nonces to prevent replay attacks.

Fail Closed by Default: In the event of an authentication service failure, unexpected exception, or missing policy decision, the security layer must deny access, revoke credentials, and log a high-priority alert.

failureModes.name: JWT Alg: None / Key Confusion Vulnerability
failureModes.description: An API gateway verifies JSON Web Tokens signed with HMAC-SHA256 using an asymmetric RSA public key, or accepts tokens with "alg": "none", allowing attackers to forge arbitrary admin claims.
failureModes.mitigation: Explicitly enforce expected signing algorithms in JWT verification libraries; never dynamically infer the verification algorithm from the untrusted token header.

failureModes.name: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Cloud Metadata Breach
failureModes.description: A webhook or avatar upload endpoint allows users to supply arbitrary URLs. An attacker provides http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ to steal AWS IAM instance credentials.
failureModes.mitigation: Block access to private IPv4/IPv6 ranges (RFC 1918, link-local, loopback) at the network DNS resolver level, and enforce IMDSv2 token authentication.

failureModes.name: Hardcoded Secret Leakage in Source Control
failureModes.description: A developer commits a database password or API private key into a git repository. Automated bots scrape public and private repos and compromise the infrastructure within 60 seconds.
failureModes.mitigation: Deploy pre-commit secret scanners (TruffleHog/GitGuardian) and transition to dynamic short-lived credentials generated on-demand by HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager.

failureModes.name: Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR)
failureModes.description: An endpoint /api/documents/12345 checks that the user is logged in, but fails to check whether document 12345 belongs to the requesting user's organization.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce object-level authorization (ABAC/OPA) in the data access layer: scope queries with WHERE id = :id AND organization_id = :current_user_org.

whenToUse: Every application that stores, processes, or transmits confidential user data, financial records, or credentials.
Distributed microservice architectures requiring secure service-to-service communication across multi-tenant clusters.
Public-facing APIs requiring secure third-party authentication and delegated access tokens (OAuth2/OIDC).
Enterprises subject to regulatory compliance frameworks (SOC2, ISO 27001, PCI-DSS, HIPAA, GDPR).
whenNotToUse: Home-brewed custom cryptography algorithms: never implement your own AES or RSA algorithms; use standard, audited libraries (libsodium, WebCrypto).
Applying complex OAuth2 client-credential token exchanges for internal in-memory function calls within the same monolithic process.
Security by obscurity: hiding endpoints or relying on unguessable URLs instead of enforcing explicit cryptographic authentication.
Encrypting low-cardinality, non-sensitive static assets (such as public marketing images) with high-overhead per-request key decryption.

tradeOffs.factor: Stateful Session Cookies vs Stateless JWTs
tradeOffs.pro: Stateless JWTs eliminate database lookups at the API gateway and scale seamlessly across distributed multi-region services.
tradeOffs.con: Stateless JWTs cannot be revoked instantly without maintaining a distributed revocation blacklist, complicating emergency logout flows.

tradeOffs.factor: mTLS Service Mesh vs Application-Layer API Keys
tradeOffs.pro: mTLS sidecars transparently encrypt all wire traffic and enforce cryptographic certificates with zero application code changes.

tradeOffs.pro: RBAC is simple to understand, model, and evaluate for standard organization structures (admin, editor, viewer).
tradeOffs.con: RBAC causes role explosion in complex multi-tenant domains; ABAC (e.g. OPA/Cedar) allows dynamic policies but requires policy engine infrastructure.

domainContent.title: Security & Identity

spark.summary: Application and infrastructure security establishes the cryptographic identity, transport integrity, delegated authorization, and policy enforcement invariants of distributed platforms. It spans TLS 1.3 and PKI, zero-trust mTLS service meshes, OAuth 2.0/OIDC federation, hardened JWT validation, phishing-resistant MFA, and decoupled RBAC/ABAC policy engines.
spark.keyTakeaway: Assume the internal network is already compromised. Eliminate ambient IP trust, enforce cryptographic identity (mTLS) and least privilege at every hop, validate token claims and algorithms strictly, and fail closed by default.

domain.purpose: Learn to architect systems where cryptographic identity, bounded delegation, and least-privilege authorization hold even when perimeter firewalls fail or internal workloads are compromised.
audience: Software and platform engineers designing authentication, authorization, and service-to-service trust.
Backend engineers hardening APIs, OAuth 2.0/OIDC flows, and JWT verification boundaries.
Staff engineers and technical leads establishing zero-trust architecture and compliance invariants.
learningOutcomes: Select appropriate cryptographic primitives (AES-GCM, ECDSA/Ed25519) and design envelope encryption with KMS.
Eliminate implicit network trust using mutual TLS (mTLS) and SPIFFE/SPIRE workload attestation.
Implement OAuth 2.1 Authorization Code + PKCE, Client Credentials, and RFC 8693 Token Exchange safely.
Separate authentication (OIDC ID Tokens) from authorization (OAuth Access Tokens) and automate JWKS rotation.
Harden JWT verification against algorithm confusion, missing claims, and token replay or leakage.
Replace phishable SMS/password flows with origin-bound FIDO2/WebAuthn passkeys and risk-based step-up auth.
Decouple authorization logic from application code using RBAC, ABAC, OPA, or Zanzibar-style relation graphs.

learningJourney.title: Cryptographic Foundations & TLS / PKI Infrastructure
learningJourney.purpose: Understand how symmetric AEAD ciphers, asymmetric signatures, X.509 PKI chains, and TLS 1.3 establish confidentiality, integrity, and server authenticity on hostile networks.
learningJourney.explanation: Modern transport and data security combines asymmetric cryptography (ECDSA, Ed25519, RSA) for identity verification and ephemeral key exchange (ECDHE) with symmetric Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AES-256-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) for wire-speed bulk encryption. TLS 1.3 removes legacy cipher suites, mandates forward secrecy via ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, encrypts the handshake after ServerHello, and reduces setup to 1-RTT (with optional 0-RTT resumption that requires strict replay protection). At rest, envelope encryption pairs per-record Data Encryption Keys (DEKs) with Key Management Service (KMS) Key Encryption Keys (KEKs) so root keys never leave hardware security modules.

benefits: Hardware-accelerated (AES-NI) throughput at tens of gigabits per second.
Provides both confidentiality and tamper-detection via authentication tags.
costs: Requires a secure out-of-band mechanism to share or wrap keys.
Nonce reuse under the same key catastrophically breaks confidentiality and integrity.

benefits: Separates public verification keys from private signing keys.
Enables verifiable X.509 certificate chains rooted in trusted CAs.
costs: Orders of magnitude slower than symmetric ciphers for bulk payloads.
Requires automated certificate lifecycle management, revocation (OCSP stapling), and rotation.

ideas.title: TLS 1.3 1-RTT and 0-RTT Resumption
ideas.description: TLS 1.3 negotiates ECDHE key shares in the initial ClientHello/ServerHello round trip for forward secrecy. 0-RTT early data avoids a round trip on resumed sessions but is vulnerable to replay attacks, so it must be restricted to strictly idempotent requests.

ideas.title: Envelope Encryption with KMS
ideas.description: Generate a unique 256-bit DEK per tenant or object, encrypt the payload locally with AES-GCM, and wrap the DEK using a KMS-managed KEK. This bounds blast radius, avoids sending bulk data over the network to KMS, and supports instant key rotation.

example.title: Eliminating 0-RTT Replay Risk on a Payment Gateway
example.scenario: After enabling TLS 1.3 0-RTT early data on edge load balancers to shave latency, a payment API observed occasional duplicate POST /v1/charges executions when mobile clients reconnected across cellular towers.
example.reasoning: TLS 1.3 0-RTT packets are not protected against network-level replay because the server has not yet contributed fresh entropy. The team disabled 0-RTT for all non-GET methods at the Envoy edge proxy and enforced idempotency keys on state-mutating endpoints.
example.lesson: Transport optimizations like 0-RTT must respect application-layer idempotency invariants; never allow replayable early data on mutating routes.

caveats: Never implement custom cryptographic primitives or use ECB mode; rely on audited libraries such as libsodium, BoringSSL, or WebCrypto.
Monitor certificate expiration continuously; an expired intermediate or leaf X.509 cert causes total service blackouts.
reflectionQuestions: Which data paths require forward secrecy in transit versus envelope encryption at rest?
How are AES-GCM nonces generated to guarantee uniqueness across distributed writers?
What happens to mutating endpoints if TLS 1.3 0-RTT early data is enabled at the CDN or load balancer?
How quickly can an intermediate CA or KMS KEK be rotated if a private key is suspected compromised?

learningJourney.title: Zero-Trust Architecture & Mutual TLS (mTLS)
learningJourney.purpose: Replace implicit perimeter and IP-based trust with cryptographic workload identity and bi-directional mTLS authentication across every network hop.
learningJourney.explanation: Zero-Trust Architecture (ZTA) assumes the corporate or cloud VPC network is already compromised. Instead of trusting requests based on source IP or subnet, every service-to-service RPC must establish mutual TLS (mTLS), where both client and server present and verify X.509 certificates signed by an internal Certificate Authority. Frameworks such as SPIFFE and SPIRE attest workloads using kernel-level metadata (Kubernetes ServiceAccount tokens, AWS Nitro/TPM attestation, cgroup IDs) and issue short-lived X.509 SVIDs (1-hour to 24-hour TTLs) rotated automatically without restarts.

architectureFlow.name: Workload Attestation (SPIRE Agent)
architectureFlow.description: Verifies pod/process identity via kubelet, cgroups, or cloud instance identity documents.

architectureFlow.name: Short-Lived X.509 SVID Issuance
architectureFlow.description: Mints a SPIFFE ID certificate (e.g., spiffe://prod.internal/ns/payments/sa/ledger) with automated rotation.

architectureFlow.name: mTLS Sidecar / Proxy Handshake
architectureFlow.description: Both caller and callee Envoy proxies validate SAN SPIFFE IDs and encrypt wire traffic.

architectureFlow.name: L7 Authorization Policy Enforcement
architectureFlow.description: Evaluates whether the verified source SPIFFE ID is permitted to invoke the target HTTP/gRPC method.

ideas.title: Short-Lived Certificates Over Static CRLs
ideas.description: Issuing 1-hour X.509 SVIDs via SPIRE or Istio Citadel reduces the window of a stolen key without relying on brittle, high-latency Certificate Revocation Lists.

ideas.title: Defense-in-Depth: L3/L4 Network Policy + L7 mTLS
ideas.description: Pair eBPF/Cilium L3/L4 deny-all network policies with L7 mTLS identity checks so compromised pods cannot even open TCP sockets to unrelated namespaces.

example.title: Containing Lateral Movement in a Multi-Tenant Kubernetes Cluster
example.scenario: A vulnerability in a public-facing image-thumbnailing pod allowed remote code execution, and the attacker immediately scanned internal 10.0.0.0/8 IPs to reach the billing database and internal admin APIs.
example.reasoning: The platform replaced flat VPC trust with Cilium default-deny L4 policies and Istio strict mTLS using SPIFFE identities. Even with shell access inside the thumbnailer pod, TCP connections to the billing namespace were dropped at the kernel eBPF layer and unauthenticated HTTP calls were rejected by Envoy.
example.lesson: IP addresses are ephemeral and spoofable; cryptographic workload identity paired with default-deny network policies stops lateral movement.

caveats: Enforce STRICT mTLS only after migrating all legacy health checks and cron jobs; PERMISSIVE mode leaves plaintext downgrade paths open.
Account for ~1-2ms sidecar proxy latency and CPU overhead on high-fanout East-West gRPC paths.
reflectionQuestions: Which internal services currently trust callers solely by VPC CIDR or Kubernetes namespace?
How are workload identities attested at boot without embedding static bootstrap secrets in container images?
What happens to East-West traffic if the internal CA or SPIRE server becomes temporarily unreachable?
Are L7 policies restricting specific HTTP verbs/paths per caller identity, or merely validating that a certificate is signed by the cluster CA?

learningJourney.title: OAuth 2.0 Authorization & Token Exchange
learningJourney.purpose: Design delegated API authorization using OAuth 2.1 Authorization Code + PKCE, Client Credentials for M2M traffic, Refresh Token rotation, and RFC 8693 Token Exchange.
learningJourney.explanation: OAuth 2.0 separates the Resource Owner, Client, Authorization Server, and Resource Server so applications can obtain scoped, time-bounded access tokens without ever handling user credentials. Modern OAuth 2.1 deprecates the Implicit and Resource Owner Password Credentials flows in favor of Authorization Code Flow with Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE, RFC 7636), which binds the token exchange to a dynamic SHA-256 code_challenge so intercepted authorization codes cannot be redeemed. For machine-to-machine (M2M) workloads, Client Credentials with private_key_jwt or mTLS client authentication replaces shared static secrets, while RFC 8693 Token Exchange enables downstream services to downscope or swap tokens across trust boundaries.

communicationChoices.useWhen: A human user delegates access to a web, SPA, or native mobile client.
A backend daemon or service calls an API on its own behalf without a user.
designFor: Asymmetric private_key_jwt or mTLS client auth.

communicationChoices.useWhen: An internal microservice needs a downscoped token to call a downstream service on the user's behalf.

ideas.title: Refresh Token Rotation with Reuse Detection
ideas.description: Issue single-use refresh tokens that rotate on every redemption. If an already-consumed refresh token is replayed, the Authorization Server immediately revokes the entire token family to contain theft.

ideas.title: Sender-Constrained Tokens (DPoP / mTLS)
ideas.description: Standard bearer tokens grant access to anyone who possesses them. Binding tokens to a client's TLS certificate (RFC 8705) or DPoP proof key prevents stolen tokens from being replayed from another host.

example.title: Stopping Authorization Code Interception in Native Mobile Apps
example.scenario: A mobile banking app used a custom URL scheme (myapp://callback) without PKCE. Malicious apps installed on the same device registered the identical scheme and intercepted the OAuth authorization code.
example.reasoning: The team migrated to OAuth 2.1 Authorization Code + PKCE (S256) and OS-verified Universal Links / App Links. Even if an attacker intercepted the authorization code, the Authorization Server rejected the /token request because the attacker lacked the ephemeral code_verifier.
example.lesson: Public clients cannot keep a client_secret confidential; PKCE and exact OS-verified redirect URIs are mandatory to bind authorization codes to the legitimate client instance.

reflectionQuestions: Are any legacy SPAs or mobile clients still using the deprecated OAuth Implicit flow instead of Authorization Code + PKCE?
How does the Authorization Server detect and respond if a rotated refresh token is replayed?
When Service A calls Service B on behalf of a user, is the raw user token forwarded blindly or downscoped via RFC 8693?
Are redirect_uri checks exact string matches, or do open-redirect wildcards allow token exfiltration?

learningJourney.title: OpenID Connect (OIDC) & Federated Identity
learningJourney.purpose: Authenticate users cleanly using OIDC ID Tokens, discovery metadata, JWKS key rotation, and enterprise SSO federation without conflating identity with API permissions.
learningJourney.explanation: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization protocol and intentionally says nothing about who the user is. OpenID Connect (OIDC) layers authentication on top of OAuth 2.0 by introducing the signed ID Token (a JWT containing sub, iss, aud, exp, iat, and nonce claims), the /userinfo endpoint, and standardized /.well-known/openid-configuration discovery. Resource servers must never accept an ID Token as an API access token, and clients must never treat an opaque OAuth Access Token as proof of user identity. For enterprise B2B SaaS, OIDC and SAML 2.0 enable federated Single Sign-On (SSO) where the customer's Identity Provider (Okta, Entra ID) remains the source of truth for user lifecycle and offboarding.

benefits: Cryptographically signed assertion of who authenticated, when, and against which issuer.
Bound to the requesting client via aud and protected from replay via nonce.
costs: Intended solely for the client application; must never be sent to backend resource servers as a bearer API credential.

benefits: Carries scoped permissions (scope) and target resource audience (aud) for API authorization.
Can be short-lived and independently refreshed or introspected.
costs: Does not guarantee the user is currently present or authenticated in the client session.

ideas.title: Dynamic Key Rotation via JWKS and kid
ideas.description: Publish public signing keys at the discovery jwks_uri with a Key ID (kid). Relying parties cache JWKS with a bounded TTL and refresh on an unknown kid, enabling zero-downtime key rotation.

ideas.title: Federated Identity Linking and Account Takeover Prevention
ideas.description: Never auto-link a federated OIDC login to an existing local account solely by an unverified email claim; require email_verified=true and explicit user confirmation or immutable (iss, sub) pair matching.

example.title: Preventing Cross-Tenant Account Takeover via Unverified Email Linking
example.scenario: A B2B SaaS platform linked incoming OIDC logins to existing user accounts by matching the email claim. An attacker created an account on an external OIDC provider with a victim's corporate email and gained access to the victim's workspace.
example.reasoning: Engineering changed the identity store to key federated identities strictly on the immutable composite (iss, sub) tuple, enforced email_verified=true, and required an authenticated step-up session before linking a new IdP to an existing local account.
example.lesson: Email addresses are mutable and not universally verified across IdPs; always key federated identity on (iss, sub).

reflectionQuestions: Does your backend API reject OIDC ID Tokens when presented in Authorization: Bearer headers?
How are user accounts keyed in the database—by mutable email or by immutable (iss, sub) pairs?
If an IdP rotates its signing key unexpectedly, does your JWKS cache fetch the new kid safely without triggering a thundering herd?
When an enterprise employee is offboarded in Okta or Entra ID, how quickly are their active application sessions terminated?

learningJourney.title: JSON Web Tokens (JWT) Architecture & Hardening
learningJourney.purpose: Eliminate signature, key-confusion, claim-validation, and browser-storage vulnerabilities in stateless JWT architectures, and design bounded revocation.
learningJourney.explanation: JSON Web Tokens (JWS for signed tokens, JWE for encrypted tokens) allow distributed services to verify claims locally without a central session database lookup. However, trusting untrusted headers or skipping claim checks leads to catastrophic bypasses: accepting "alg": "none" disables signature verification entirely, while RS256-to-HS256 key confusion tricks a server into verifying an HMAC signature using its publicly known RSA public key. Hardened JWT verification pins an explicit algorithm allowlist on the server, validates iss, aud, exp, and nbf with bounded clock skew, stores tokens in HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite cookies rather than localStorage (to resist XSS exfiltration), and pairs short 5-15 minute access TTLs with a Redis jti revocation blocklist for emergency logouts.

ideas.title: Explicit Server-Side Algorithm Pinning
ideas.description: Configure JWT verifiers with an explicit allowlist (e.g., ["RS256", "ES256"]). Never derive the verification algorithm from the untrusted JWT header's alg field.

ideas.title: Short TTLs + Bounded JTI Revocation Blocklist
ideas.description: Keep access token lifetimes to 5-15 minutes so a Redis revocation set keyed by jti only needs to store revoked IDs until their natural exp timestamp, bounding memory growth.

example.title: Closing an RS256/HS256 Key Confusion Bypass in an API Gateway
example.scenario: A penetration test forged an admin JWT accepted by a Node.js API gateway by signing an admin payload with HS256 using the gateway's publicly downloadable RSA public key as the HMAC secret.
example.reasoning: The gateway's verification middleware passed the JWKS RSA public key directly to jwt.verify() without specifying algorithms: ["RS256"]. Pinning algorithms: ["RS256"] and enforcing strict iss and aud validation eliminated the forgery vector immediately.
example.lesson: A JWT header is attacker-controlled input; always pin expected algorithms and validate every standard claim server-side.

caveats: Signed JWS payloads are Base64URL-encoded, not encrypted; never put PII, secrets, or internal database IDs in a JWS without JWE encryption.
If the Redis jti blocklist is unreachable during an emergency revocation check, fail closed on high-privilege endpoints.
reflectionQuestions: Does every JWT verification call in your codebase explicitly pin allowed signing algorithms?
Are both iss and aud validated so tokens issued for one microservice cannot be replayed against another?
Where are tokens stored in the browser—and if in localStorage, what prevents an XSS payload from exfiltrating them?
How long can a compromised user's access token remain valid after password reset or account suspension?

learningJourney.title: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) & Risk-Based Security
learningJourney.purpose: Move beyond phishable passwords and SMS codes to cryptographic FIDO2/WebAuthn passkeys, hardened TOTP (RFC 6238), and adaptive step-up authentication.
learningJourney.explanation: Multi-Factor Authentication combines independent evidence across knowledge (passwords), possession (hardware keys, authenticator apps), and inherence (biometrics). SMS and voice OTPs are vulnerable to SIM swapping, SS7 interception, and real-time adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing proxies. TOTP (RFC 6238) improves on SMS by computing HMAC-SHA1/256 over 30-second time steps with a ±1 window for clock skew and strict single-use replay tracking, though it remains phishable on lookalike domains. FIDO2/WebAuthn passkeys eliminate phishing entirely by using asymmetric device keys where the browser cryptographically binds the signed challenge to the exact TLS origin (rpId).

benefits: Zero app installation required; broad reach.
costs: Vulnerable to SIM swapping, carrier social engineering, and SS7 interception.
Easily captured by AiTM phishing proxies.

benefits: Works offline without telecom carrier dependencies.
Simple server-side verification with ±1 step drift tolerance.
costs: Shared secret can still be phished by real-time reverse-proxy phishing kits.
Requires single-use code tracking to prevent replay within the 30s window.

benefits: Cryptographically bound to the exact origin (rpId), defeating AiTM phishing.
Private key never leaves the hardware enclave or synced platform keychain.
costs: Requires account recovery workflows when a user loses all registered devices.

ideas.title: Single-Use TOTP Replay Prevention
ideas.description: Record the last accepted TOTP time-step counter per user in Redis or the auth database and reject any subsequent attempt using the same or older time step.

ideas.title: Adaptive Risk-Based Step-Up Authentication
ideas.description: Evaluate device posture, impossible travel, IP reputation, and action sensitivity (e.g., wire transfer, API key creation) to trigger WebAuthn step-up challenges without adding friction to routine reads.

example.title: Defeating AiTM Phishing Proxies with FIDO2 Origin Binding
example.scenario: Employees using passwords and TOTP codes fell victim to a reverse-proxy phishing site (login-corp-sso.com) that relayed credentials and valid 6-digit TOTP codes in real time to the real IdP.
example.reasoning: The security team mandated hardware-backed FIDO2 WebAuthn passkeys for all corporate SSO logins. When an employee visited the phishing domain, the browser signed the WebAuthn challenge with the phishing rpId, which the real IdP rejected because it did not match the canonical origin.
example.lesson: Only cryptographic origin-bound factors like FIDO2/WebAuthn stop real-time adversary-in-the-middle phishing proxies.

reflectionQuestions: Which high-risk user or admin actions still rely on SMS OTP or allow password-only access?
Does your TOTP verifier prevent the same 6-digit code from being replayed within its 30-second validity window?
How does your WebAuthn recovery flow verify identity without reintroducing a weaker fallback factor that bypasses passkey security?
What risk signals trigger step-up authentication mid-session (e.g., ASN change, new device, privilege escalation)?

learningJourney.title: Authorization Models: RBAC, ABAC & Policy as Code
learningJourney.purpose: Prevent IDOR and role explosion by decoupling authorization into RBAC, ABAC, Policy-as-Code (OPA/Cedar), and Zanzibar relationship graphs.
learningJourney.explanation: Authentication proves who the caller is; authorization decides what they may do on a specific resource. Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) maps users to static roles (admin, editor, viewer) and works well for coarse-grained permissions, but suffers role explosion in multi-tenant B2B apps where access depends on ownership, department, time, or data classification. Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) evaluates dynamic subject, resource, action, and environment attributes using externalized Policy-as-Code engines like Open Policy Agent (OPA/Rego) or AWS Cedar. For deeply nested hierarchical sharing (folders, teams, documents), Relationship-Based Access Control (ReBAC / Google Zanzibar) evaluates transitive permission graphs with bounded latency.

ideas.title: Object-Level Authorization to Prevent IDOR
ideas.description: Never check only that a user has a role like 'member'; always enforce resource ownership or tenant scoping (e.g., WHERE doc_id = :id AND tenant_id = :token_tenant) at the data-access boundary.

ideas.title: Decoupled Policy-as-Code (OPA / Cedar)
ideas.description: Externalize authorization rules from application code into versioned, unit-tested Rego or Cedar policies evaluated via an embedded library or local sidecar with <1ms p99 latency.

example.title: Eliminating Role Explosion and IDOR in a Multi-Tenant SaaS
example.scenario: A B2B analytics platform had accumulated 140 custom RBAC roles per customer to model workspace, folder, and dashboard permissions, while an un-scoped /api/reports/:id endpoint leaked cross-tenant reports (IDOR).
example.reasoning: The team replaced ad-hoc role checks with a unified Policy-as-Code layer (OPA) paired with a Zanzibar-style relation graph (user -> team -> folder -> report). Every API handler queried the policy engine with (subject, action, resource_id, tenant_id), eliminating both role explosion and IDOR.
example.lesson: Coarse RBAC cannot express resource-level ownership cleanly; pair RBAC with ABAC or ReBAC at every object access boundary.

reasoning: Enforce TLS 1.3 at the edge and disable 0-RTT on mutating endpoints to eliminate transport-level replay.
Require Authorization Code + PKCE for user apps, FIDO2 WebAuthn step-up for wire transfers, and private_key_jwt for B2B partner clients.
Pin JWT verification algorithms server-side, validate iss/aud/exp, and bound token lifetime to 10 minutes with a Redis jti revocation set.
Attest internal microservices with SPIFFE/SPIRE and enforce strict mTLS plus Cilium L4 network policies so compromised pods cannot pivot.
Use RFC 8693 Token Exchange for downstream calls so services only receive the minimal scopes and audience they need.
Externalize tenant and object-level authorization into unit-tested OPA policies so IDOR is prevented uniformly at the data boundary.
lessons: Transport security, authentication, and authorization are distinct layers; weakness in any single layer compromises the whole chain.
Never trust internal VPC IPs or unverified JWT headers; verify cryptographic identity and explicit claims at every boundary.
Short-lived credentials (SVIDs, 10-minute JWTs, KMS-rotated DEKs) bound the blast radius of inevitable credential leaks.
Phishing-resistant FIDO2/WebAuthn and origin-bound tokens protect high-value actions where passwords and SMS fail.
Fail closed by default: an unreachable policy engine or revocation store must deny access rather than silently allowing it.

knowledgeCheck.question: A mobile banking app uses OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow without PKCE and verifies incoming JWTs at the API gateway without pinning allowed algorithms. Which combined vulnerability posture does this create?

options.text: Malicious apps can intercept authorization codes on custom URI schemes, and attackers can forge admin JWTs via alg:none or RS256-to-HS256 key confusion.
options.feedback: Correct. Public mobile clients require PKCE (S256) to bind authorization codes to the client instance, and JWT verifiers must pin an explicit algorithm allowlist.

options.text: The app is secure as long as traffic runs over TLS 1.3, because TLS encrypts the JWT header and redirect URI.
options.feedback: TLS protects data on the wire, not against a malicious app intercepting an OS custom URI scheme or an attacker crafting a forged JWT header.

options.text: Switching from RS256 to HS256 with a shared secret across all mobile clients solves both issues.
options.feedback: Embedding an HMAC secret inside a public mobile binary allows anyone to extract it and mint arbitrary tokens.

steps.explanation: **JWT Key Confusion + Compromised Internal Pod** — An attacker exploits an SSRF or dependency vulnerability in a non-critical reporting pod and attempts to both forge an admin JWT via alg:none/HS256 confusion and connect directly to the ledger database. **Recovery:** Pinned algorithm allowlists reject the forged JWT at the gateway, Cilium L4 policies drop direct TCP packets from the reporting pod to the ledger DB, and strict mTLS + OPA deny any unauthorized RPCs while alerting SOC telemetry.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Assume the internal network is already compromised. Eliminate ambient IP trust, enforce cryptographic identity (mTLS) and least privilege at every hop, validate token claims and algorithms strictly, and fail closed by default.
